verses.note: In Israel the offices of king and priest were kept apart, and kings who took priestly roles were rebuked (2 Chronicles 26:16-18). Melchizedek holds both at once, which is why Scripture can use him to describe the Messiah's joined kingship and priesthood.

The first person Scripture calls a prophet is Abraham, and what defines him here is not prediction but nearness to God and the right to plead for others. That shape of the prophetic office runs through the Old Testament and is fulfilled in Christ, who always lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25).

Aaron's marriage joins the priestly line to the house of Nahshon, whose descendant David will found Israel's royal line (Ruth 4:20-22; Matthew 1:4-6). The Old Testament keeps the offices of priest and king separate, but the two families are joined here; the New Testament presents Jesus as fulfilling both offices (Hebrews 7:14-17).

Moses stands between God and the people as prophet, speaking God's words to them. Deuteronomy 18:15-18 remembers this request as the origin of the prophetic office and promises a prophet like Moses, whom the New Testament identifies with Jesus (Acts 3:22-23).

Moses mediates God's words to the people as he did at the first giving of the law. The fear his face provokes is the same fear the people felt at God's voice (20:19), and it is answered the same way: God's word comes to them through the mediator.

On this one day the high priest sets aside the gold and jewels of his office (Exodus 28) and enters in plain linen. His representative role is most complete when his personal splendor is removed, and he must first deal with his own sin before he can act for others.
The mediator acts alone, unseen, on behalf of all. Hebrews reads Christ's work in these terms: he entered the true sanctuary alone and appears there on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24).

The high priest's office passes from father to son, and each dies in turn. Hebrews builds its argument on this: the former priests were many because death prevented them from continuing, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever (Hebrews 7:23-25).
The priesthood is set apart from the ordinary economy of land and inheritance. Those who serve at the altar are meant to depend on God and on the worship of his people, not on estates of their own.

Christian theology has named prophet as one of Christ's three offices, with priest and king. Jesus' claim in John 12:49-50 that he speaks just what the Father commanded him echoes the language of this verse.

The verse joins kingship and priesthood in one person by divine oath. The church's teaching that Christ holds the offices of prophet, priest, and king (set out at length by Calvin, Institutes 2.15) finds one of its main Old Testament roots here.

Jesus calls himself a prophet. Christian theology has spoken of Christ as prophet, priest, and king (the threefold office set out by Calvin, Institutes 2.15); this verse is one of the places the prophetic office is claimed, together with its cost.

Jesus blesses his people as a priest and is taken up to heaven, where, as Hebrews says, he lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25). The church has spoken of Christ's threefold office as prophet, priest, and king; Luke's last picture shows the priest whose blessing continues from heaven.

The first title the woman gives Jesus is prophet, and it is not wrong, only incomplete. John shows Jesus fulfilling the prophetic office of speaking God's word and knowing hearts, on the way to the fuller confessions of Messiah (verse 26) and Savior (verse 42).

The crowd names Jesus the Prophet like Moses, one of the three offices (prophet, priest, and king) in which the church has summarized Christ's work. The next verse shows the danger of honoring one office on one's own terms: they want the prophet to become their kind of king.

The titles in the crowd's debate, Prophet and Christ, name two of the offices that Christians later saw united in Jesus. The crowd treats them as alternatives; the Gospel shows him to be both, and more.
The man reaches for the office Israel knew for a man through whom God acted: prophet. It is a true title (Luke 24:19), and it is not the last he will use.

Paul's authority rests on a commission, not on personal gifts or standing. The verse defines the apostle as one sent and set apart by God for a message he did not invent, which is why the letter can speak with authority to a church Paul did not found.
Ministry is described as stewardship, a trust given by God and exercised for the sake of the church. Paul's authority is derivative: he administers what belongs to God.
Jesus' office as high priest is introduced here. The Reformers spoke of Christ's threefold office as prophet, priest, and king, and Hebrews supplies more of the priestly part than any other book.

Jesus is apostle (God's envoy, like Moses) and high priest (the people's representative, like Aaron) at once. The two roles that Israel's history divided between two brothers are united in one person.
Jesus is high priest as the Son of God who has entered God's presence. His priesthood is not an earthly office but the ministry of the exalted Son in heaven itself (8:1-2, 9:24).

The verse defines priesthood by solidarity and representation: a priest must be one of the people and act for them. That is why Hebrews insists on the full humanity of the Son (2:14-17). Only one who shares human nature can hold this office on humanity's behalf.
A priesthood that does not depend on descent is the author's point. The Son's priesthood rests on who he is and on God's oath, not on a family tree, which is why it cannot pass to another.

Tithe and blessing both mark rank. By receiving a tithe from Abraham and blessing him, Melchizedek shows himself greater than the ancestor of every Levitical priest, and so his kind of priesthood outranks theirs.

In Israel king and priest were separate offices, and kings who seized priestly functions were judged (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). In Jesus, from the royal tribe, the two offices are united by God's appointment, as Zechariah 6:13 had pictured a priest on the throne.
The law's priests were weak men; God's oath installed a perfected Son. The verse compresses the letter's whole case for the superiority of Christ's priesthood into one sentence.
Priest and mediator coincide in Christ. The one who offers the sacrifice is the one who establishes the covenant it seals, which the old order divided between Aaron and Moses.
